message.content:
Nicolaus Copernicus faced criticism from several prominent figures in the late sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries. Martin Luther, the Protestant reformer, dismissed the heliocentric model as a dangerous departure from Scripture, calling it a "new madness." Philipp Melanchthon, Luther's close associate, raised theological objections about how the theory conflicted with passages describing a stationary Earth. The Catholic Church, through Cardinal Cesare Baronius, eventually placed *De Revolutionibus* on the Index of Forbidden Books in 1616.

Who would dare challenge the centuries-old Ptolemaic system so fundamentally? Did not the Bible clearly describe a fixed Earth at the center of God's creation? How could scholars reconcile the proposed motion of the Earth with the teachings of scripture? Was it not perilous to overturn a cosmology that had stood for over a millennium?

How audacious the Copernican proposal truly was in its own era! What a formidable challenge it presented to both the intellectual and religious establishment! Surely no one could dismiss so carefully constructed a model without careful cause! What remarkable courage Copernicus displayed in publishing his work despite the mounting opposition around him!
